prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Still, citizen sparrow, this vulture which you call Unnatural, let him but lumber again to air Over the rotten office, let him bear The carrion ballast up, and at the tall Tip of the sky lie cruising. Then you’ll see That no more beautiful bird is in heaven’s height, No wider more placid wings, no watchfuller flight; He shoulders nature there, the frightfully free, The naked-headed one. Pardon him, you Who dart in the orchard aisles, for it is he Devours death, mocks mutability, Has heart to make an end, keeps nature new. Thinking of Noah, childheart, try to forget How for so many bedlam hours his saw Soured the song of birds with its wheezy gnaw, And the slam of his hammer all the day beset The people’s ears. Forget that he could bear To see the towns like coral under the keel, And the fields so dismal deep. Try rather to feel How high and weary it was, on the waters where He rocked his only world, and everyone’s. Forgive the hero, you who would have died Gladly with all you knew; he rode that tide To Ararat; all men are Noah’s sons.

Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker urges the sparrow to reconsider the vulture, arguing that it appears beautiful and natural when seen soaring in the sky.
- The vulture is portrayed as a necessary creature that consumes death, resists decay, and helps renew nature.
- The speaker asks the childlike listener to forgive Noah for the noise and disruption caused by building the ark.
- Noah’s survival is presented as lonely and burdensome because he carried the fate of the world through the flood.
- The poem suggests that Noah should be forgiven as a hero because all humanity descends from him.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Still, Unnatural, Over

outputs.L1:
Still, citizen sparrow, this vulture which you call  
Unnatural—let him but lumber again to air  
Over the rotten office; let him bear  
The carrion ballast up, and at the tall  
Tip of the sky lie cruising. Then you’ll see  
That no more beautiful bird is in heaven’s height,  
No wider, more placid wings, no watchfuller flight.  
He shoulders nature there, the frightfully free,  
The naked-headed one. Pardon him, you  
Who dart in the orchard aisles, for it is he  
Who devours death, mocks mutability,  
Has heart to make an end, and keeps nature new.  

Thinking of Noah, childheart, try to forget  
How, for so many bedlam hours, his saw  
Soured the song of birds with its wheezy gnaw,  
And the slam of his hammer all the day beset  
The people’s ears. Forget that he could bear  
To see the towns like coral under the keel,  
And the fields so dismal deep. Try rather to feel  
How high and weary it was, on the waters where  
He rocked his only world, and everyone’s.  
Forgive the hero, you who would have died  
Gladly with all you knew; he rode that tide  
To Ararat; all men are Noah’s sons.
outputs.L2:
Even so, little civic-minded sparrow: the scavenger you condemn as “unnatural” should be allowed to heave himself back into the air above the decaying workplace. Let him lift that dead weight of carrion and glide near the sky’s highest edge. From there, you would recognize that no bird aloft is more splendid—none has broader, calmer wings or a more vigilant way of flying. Up there, bald-headed and terrifyingly free, he takes on nature’s necessary burden. Forgive him, you quick orchard-flitterer, because he consumes death, defies decay, has the courage to finish what must end, and helps keep the natural world renewed.

And when you think of Noah, tender-hearted one, try not to dwell on those countless mad hours when the rasping bite of his saw spoiled the birds’ music, or on the hammer blows that battered everyone’s ears all day long. Try to forget that he was able to watch towns sink beneath his vessel like coral, and fields disappear into dreadful depths. Instead, try to imagine how lonely, exhausted, and elevated his life was upon those waters, where he carried the only remaining world—his own, and everyone else’s. Forgive that hero, you who would willingly have perished with all you loved and knew; he endured the flood and reached Ararat, and every human being descends from Noah.
outputs.L3:
The speaker urges the sparrow to look again at the vulture and to reconsider its first judgment. Although the bird may seem ugly or frightening when seen up close, it becomes beautiful and natural when it is viewed high in the sky, soaring as it was meant to do. From that distance, the vulture appears graceful, powerful, and fully at home in the world.

The poem also presents the vulture as a necessary part of nature. It is not merely a symbol of death, but a creature that performs an important task: it consumes what is dead, resists decay, and helps return life to the natural cycle. By feeding on death, the vulture helps cleanse the earth and make renewal possible. In this way, something that may seem unpleasant is shown to have value and purpose.

The speaker then turns to a childlike listener and asks for forgiveness for Noah. Noah may have seemed noisy, strange, and disruptive while building the ark, disturbing the peace around him with his hammering and preparations. Yet this disturbance had a greater purpose. He was preparing for the flood and for the survival of life itself.

Noah’s survival is not presented as easy or triumphant. Instead, it is lonely and burdensome. He carried the fate of the world through the flood, preserving human and animal life while everything else was destroyed. His role was heroic, but it also separated him from others and placed an immense responsibility on him.

Ultimately, the poem suggests that Noah deserves forgiveness and honor. He should be remembered as a hero because all humanity descends from him. His actions made the continuation of human life possible, and for that reason, the childlike listener is asked to forgive the disruption he caused and recognize the greatness of what he achieved.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the way certain figures, at first seen as ugly, disturbing, or unnatural, can be understood differently when viewed with patience and sympathy. The vulture, for example, is not usually admired. It is associated with death, decay, and ugliness, and its presence can seem frightening or unpleasant. Yet the poem invites the reader to look beyond this first reaction. The vulture performs an important role in the natural world: it clears away what is dead and helps restore balance. What appears repulsive on the surface is therefore connected to cleansing, renewal, and the continuation of life.

In a similar way, Noah may also seem like a disruptive or strange figure. His story is tied to destruction, flood, and the end of an old world. At first, he might appear to belong to a frightening vision of nature and divine judgment. However, the poem reconsiders him as a figure of preservation rather than simple destruction. Noah survives the flood and protects the living creatures that will repopulate the earth. Through him, life is carried forward into a new beginning.

By placing the vulture and Noah together, the poem suggests that what seems harsh, ugly, or terrifying may have a deeper purpose. Both figures are connected to death or destruction, but both also make renewal possible. The vulture transforms decay into natural balance, while Noah preserves life through catastrophe. In this way, the poem asks the reader to adopt a more forgiving and symbolic perspective. It shows that nature and survival often depend on forces that may not appear beautiful or gentle, but are necessary for the preservation of life.
outputs.L5:
**Still, Unnatural, Over**

The town was still after sunset, but not in the peaceful way people usually described silence. It was too complete, too heavy, as if the world had forgotten how to breathe.

Above the rooftops, the sky glowed an unnatural shade of violet. No stars appeared. No wind moved through the trees. Even the stray dogs, usually loud and restless, had vanished into doorways and shadows.

Mara stood in the empty street, staring at the old clock tower. Its hands had stopped at midnight, though the sun had only just disappeared. She told herself it was only a storm coming, some strange trick of the light, something ordinary with an explanation waiting just out of reach.

Then the bells began to ring.

Once. Twice. Three times.

Each sound rolled over the town like a warning.

And when the final echo faded, Mara understood with a cold certainty that whatever had begun here was not over.

It was only starting.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a formal poem in the style of mid-20th-century American verse that defends the vulture as a necessary and beautiful part of nature, then shifts into a meditation on Noah and the burden of survival.
counterfactuals.output:
**Apologia for the Vulture, with Noah**

Do not despise the vulture for his trade,  
Nor call his circling hunger a disgrace.  
He is the dark physician of the glade,  
The hooded priest of every fallen place.  

Where fever would have lifted from the slain,  
Where sweetness would have sickened into blight,  
He comes, severe as weather after rain,  
And sets corruption cleanly out of sight.  

Consider how he rides the noon’s high wheel,  
A ragged hierarch of sun and air;  
What other heart, so patient and so real,  
Can make a feast of what we cannot bear?  

His wings are tablets written on the sky,  
His shadow passes, and the grasses mend.  
He teaches every living thing to die  
Without denying death its use, its end.  

Not all that serves is lovely to the first  
Unpracticed glance; not all that saves is fair.  
The earth has instruments for blood and thirst,  
For rot, for bone, for silence, and for prayer.  

So Noah, when the waters fell away,  
Stood among cages, stunned by what remained:  
The reek of breath, the doves’ uncertain gray,  
The lion’s hunger, and the oxen drained.  

How heavy then the covenant must be—  
Not rainbow only, arched in colored flame,  
But dung and claw, the seed, the broken tree,  
The saved world crying each survivor’s name.  

To live is not to rise absolved and bright  
From wreckage, as from sleep without a scar;  
It is to feed the creatures through the night  
And learn what strange necessities they are.  

Perhaps he watched, beyond the settling ark,  
A vulture tilt above the steaming plain,  
And knew that mercy also may be dark,  
That life returns through appetite and pain.  

O keeper of the remnant, bend and see:  
The clean, the foul, are numbered in one breath.  
The world is not preserved by purity,  
But by the faithful ministries of death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed, elevated poem addressing a sparrow, arguing that the vulture is not unnatural but sacred because it consumes death and renews the world.
counterfactuals.output:
O sparrow, stitching dawn with thread of song,  
Why shrink from wings that wheel where no fields bloom?  
The vulture’s shadow, solemn, vast, and strong,  
Is not a blot upon the light of noon.  

He does not murder spring, nor mock the breath  
That stirs your breast and lifts you from the thorn;  
He is the priest of what has fallen to death,  
The dark-robed herald of a world reborn.  

Where fevered flesh would poison earth and stream,  
He stoops, and in his terrible mercy feeds;  
He drinks the ruin, sanctifies the dream,  
And leaves the clean ground ready for new seeds.  

Call not unnatural that ancient rite  
By which the sky bends low to heal the sod;  
The carrion crowned beneath his circling flight  
Becomes, through him, an offering back to God.  

So sing, small flame, but do not sing disdain:  
The holy has more faces than the rose.  
Some guard the bud, some gather up the slain,  
And both keep watch that life may decompose  

Into its glory—root and leaf and wing,  
The worm’s deep labor, and the blossom’s breath.  
Praise, then, the vulture: grave, unsonging king,  
Who eats the dead and gives the world from death.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem with biblical allusion to Noah’s Ark, asking the reader to forgive both the vulture and Noah for their harsh but necessary roles in preserving life.
counterfactuals.output:
Forgive the vulture, reader—  
his black psalm circling the drowned world,  
his beak made stern by hunger,  
his wings writing famine over the waves.  

He did not summon the rain,  
nor bargain with the thunder;  
he only kept the covenant of bone,  
turning ruin back to earth  
so something green might rise.  

And forgive Noah, too—  
old man of splinters and terror,  
shutting the door while the sky fell.  
What mercy could his hands hold  
when mercy had narrowed to a hull,  
when every breath inside the ark  
was purchased by the silence outside?  

He saved what he could:  
the lowing dark, the feathered spark,  
the seed asleep in the lion’s mane,  
the small bright pulse of olive leaves  
not yet invented by the dove.  

Judge gently, you who stand  
on land washed clean of screams.  
The flood has many servants:  
the rain that breaks, the mouth that takes,  
the man who bars the door.  

Forgive them both—  
the scavenger and the sailor—  
for life, in its torn robe,  
sometimes passes through the cruelest hands  
and still emerges  
bearing green in its teeth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate Richard Wilbur’s poetic style: write a dense, sonnet-like passage about a vulture in flight and Noah on the flood, using formal diction, moral paradox, and intricate rhyme.
counterfactuals.output:
Above the drowned world’s mild, accusing glass,  
A vulture holds his ugly grace in air,  
Where thermals, like permissions, let him pass  
On motionless amendments of despair.  

Below, the ark—black seed of what must be—  
Knocks at the hilltops, freighted with reprieve;  
And Noah, shut with dung and prophecy,  
Keeps faith with beasts he scarcely can believe.  

What carrion angel circles? Hunger’s priest,  
He sanctifies the ruin he surveys;  
By taking death to heart, he makes it least,  
And turns corruption into length of days.  

So mercy feeds on judgment, wing by wing:  
The clean dove waits; the unclean shadows sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a poem that begins “Still, citizen sparrow,” and develops into a philosophical defense of ugly or frightening agents of renewal, ending with the idea that all men are Noah’s sons.
counterfactuals.output:
Still, citizen sparrow,  
do not scold the crow for his black coat,  
nor the beetle for shouldering the world’s rot  
beneath the damp boards of the garden.

The vulture’s circle is not a curse  
but a patient geometry of mercy;  
the worm, blind and low,  
writes green futures in the grave’s dark margin.

Even fire, that red-mouthed prosecutor,  
clears the choking underbrush  
so pinecones may unlock their fists  
and seeds may leap from ruin.

We fear the agents with ragged faces:  
mold on the fallen fruit,  
storm at the harbor,  
jackal, maggot, flood.

Yet what is renewal  
but beauty arriving in work clothes,  
with mud on its boots  
and a smell we would rather not name?

The world is not kept clean by innocence.  
It is mended by hunger, weather, endings—  
by those who take the spent thing down  
so life may climb its bones.

So bless the dark-winged laborers,  
the breakers, scavengers, terrible midwives;  
for after every deluge, whatever shore we find,  
all men are Noah’s sons.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
